newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain winemaker's profit above plan as IPO starts.
newsitem.headline: Spain winemaker's profit above plan as IPO starts.

text.p: Spanish Rioja wine producer Baron de Ley, which launched its initial public offering on Wednesday, said profits so far this year were exceeding estimates.
"As of the end of May, sales and profits were above forecast," managing director and vice chairman Eduardo Santos-Ruiz told journalists after the group's first presentation.
At the end of June, sales were running 20 percent above plan. The group has budgeted for full-year 1997 pretax profit of 1.35 billion pesetas ($9.1 million), after 1996 profit of 1.31 billion.
First-quarter sales rose 19.7 percent to 990 million pesetas, while operating revenues rose 7.4 percent to 337 million pesetas.

Baron de Ley, which produces Coto de Rioja and eponymous brands from Spain's sole qualified denomination of origin, the northcentral Rioja, is selling up to 74.6 percent of its capital to domestic and foreign institutions.

The remaining share capital will remain in the hands of four top managers. In the offer, which can be taken up through July 11, the national tranche comprises 45 percent and the international, 55 percent. There is no retail tranche.

A series of top-flight harvests have helped boost Baron de Ley profits dramatically since it was created in 1991, and Santos-Ruiz conceded the group may not be able to keep up the pace of its earnings increases.
The 1994 and 1995 grape harvests won the qualification "excellent," from the Rioja Quality Control Board while 1996 was classified as "very good".
In part as a result, pre-tax profit at Baron de Ley rose to 1.31 billion last year from 677 million in 1995 or just 255 million in 1993.
"The rhythm of gains will be difficult to maintain," Santos-Ruiz said, but added that the high quality of the recent harvests would help compensate for any lower quality ones ahead.
"We want to keep the 35 percent margin of profits to sales."

Finer grapes are used to make upscale, more expensive reserve wines, which are aged for at least three years, and grand reserve wines. Lesser quality grapes are used for crianza, which requires less ageing.
Baron de Ley currently has more than 20 million litres of wine in its cellars, worth more than 8.5 billion pesetas at current market prices.
By the year 2001, following more than four million pesetas in investments, the group is aiming for sales of 14,400,000 bottles a year. In 1996, it sold 8,573,868 bottles.
As part of these investments, it foresees buying a wine maker in Spain's upcoming northern region of Ribera del Duero.

Currently, Baron de Ley has two wine production centres and some 180 hectares, planted principally with the Tempranillo grape, which is derived from Pinot Noir and considered Spain's finest black grape. It also buys grapes and fermented wines.

The initial public offering faces timing questions apart from those of the harvest. Although the Spanish bourse has been leaping from new high to new high, the global market for wine consumption has been declining.
Still, fine wine consumption, such as Baron de Ley, is climbing by one percent annually, Santos-Ruiz said.
Despite these worries, Santos-Ruiz said Baron de Ley will begin dividend payments on its 1998 year and expects its initial public offering to go well.
It will start paying interim dividends of 25 percent of net profits on 1998 results, Santos-Ruiz said.
"There aren't many wine producers listed in Europe. It's innovative, agreeable and sweet," he added.
